attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps both 'among the first' parts. It drops 'hyping them proudly', but the contract restores that. It is a retrospective observation about Klarna.

contract.note: Reading a freeze plus attrition as 'AI layoffs' is generous, but it is the ordinary reading: the media widely called these AI-driven cuts. 'Among the first' rests on prominence and timing, not exact rank. The reading is not stretched much either way.

evidence.note: Dec 2024: the CEO publicly touted AI doing the work of hundreds of staff and a hiring freeze dating to late 2023.
The 2024 claim that AI did the work of 700 agents moved a rival's stock, which marks Klarna as a prominent early case.
May 2025: the CEO said the cost focus gave lower quality and that Klarna would invest in human support.
The walkback was partial: Klarna kept shrinking headcount through attrition while it rehired support staff.
Challenger data: over 75% of AI-attributed cuts since 2023 came in 2025, after Klarna's moves. This backs the early timing.

reviews.rationale: Klarna loudly touted AI-driven workforce cuts in 2024, from a freeze that began in 2023. That was before the 2025 wave of AI-attributed cuts. In May 2025 its CEO publicly admitted lower quality and began rehiring humans. The walkback was partial and no list ranks reversal dates, but the contract's support condition is met.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence. He agrees with Garman elsewhere, but this line is in his own voice.

semantics.note: Here 'can' states ability, not a hedge. 'Often' is kept in both halves. It is an observation about AI's current ability.

contract.note: Mapping it onto 2025 work-task benchmarks is a fair plain reading. Using calendar 2025 as the period is reasonable. Junior roles and judgement are only approximated by tasks.

evidence.note: Remote Labor Index, Oct 2025: the best agent automated only 2.5% of real projects end to end, so AI often cannot do the whole job.
GDPval: the best model matched or beat experts on about 48% of tasks. So AI does some of the work and falls short of experts on the rest.
GDPval's comparison group averaged 14 years of experience, which ties it to the senior-professional half of the claim.

reviews.rationale: 2025 evaluations show AI matching experts on a real share of tasks (GDPval, about half). They also show it rarely completing whole projects (RLI, 2.5%) and falling short of seasoned professionals on most remaining tasks. That fits 'some but often not all' and 'often lacks' senior judgement. Nothing shows AI doing whole junior jobs routinely.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: Revision 2 restores 'I believe', 'all too often', both halves, and the scope. It is an opinion about employers' misjudgments, framed as an observation that cannot be measured.

contract.note: Treating it as an untestable belief about employers' internal estimates is fair. It has no threshold or measure.

evidence.note: One employer (Klarna) admitted its AI-first approach lowered quality. That is a single case and cannot test how often employers misjudge.

reviews.rationale: This is a stated belief ('I believe') that employers 'all too often' misjudge humans and AI. Employers' internal estimates cannot be observed and no frequency threshold exists. One Klarna anecdote fits the view but cannot score it.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words opening his post.

semantics.note: Both 'often' qualifiers are kept. 'License' is rendered as 'justify', and 'don't know what the hell' as 'don't understand AI'. Acceptable.

contract.note: Reading 'often' as a common, widely noted pattern is ordinary. Counting AI-washing findings toward the misjudgment half is somewhat generous, since a pretext implies knowing. But Cappelli's 'just hoping' gives some direct support.

evidence.note: Oxford Economics on 2025 data: some firms dress up layoffs as an AI story. The article also has Cappelli saying firms are just hoping AI will cover the work.
Forrester: many firms announcing AI layoffs lacked mature AI to fill the roles, a trend it calls AI-washing.
Gownder says CEOs not deep into AI are making a big mistake. It is dated Feb 2026, outside the 2025 period, so context only.
AI was cited in 4.5% of US cuts but about 55k jobs in 2025, a sharp rise. That is not 'rarely invoked', and it measures explicit attribution, not vagueness.

reviews.rationale: Independent analysts (Oxford Economics, Forrester) found that 2025 AI-attributed layoffs were commonly not backed by AI ready to do the work. They also found AI was used as a positive gloss, and Cappelli says firms were just hoping. The 4.5% share does not meet the contradiction condition. The ignorance half is rhetorical and supported more weakly.
